title: Cyrano de Bergerac
byline: José Ferrer won the Best Actor Oscar for Stanley Kramer's 1950 film of Rostand's play.

evidence.note: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures Jan-Dec 1977 (Vol 31 Nos 1-2). I searched only the portion of the volume my fetch tool returned, because the tool reads only part of a long volume. I did not confirm that the whole volume was searched. In that portion I found no occurrence of 'Cyrano'. This is a partial check and covers only the 1977 part of the renewal window. I did not check the Jan-Jun 1978 volume (archive.org/details/catalogofcopyrig14libr) or the Jul-Dec 1978 Motion Pictures volume. A renewal in the 28th year could have been filed through the end of 1978. I did not search the Copyright Office public catalog, because its page is a JavaScript app that returned no records to my fetch.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, 1977 Motion Pictures, archive.org

evidence.note: An Internet Archive uploader describes the film as 'PD due to lack of copyright renewal'. This is an uploader's claim, not a primary record. Secondary reporting (Wikipedia) says the film lapsed into the public domain in the mid-1980s. That is unverified, and no primary source is given for it. Do not rely on either claim until the Jan-Jun 1978 and Jul-Dec 1978 catalogs and the Copyright Office records have been checked.

Dimitri Tiomkin composed the score. It is a sound film, so the recorded track would normally share the film's own copyright status. Separate publishing rights in the underlying music were not checked.

Based on Edmond Rostand's 1897 French play. The screenplay uses Brian Hooker's 1923 English blank-verse translation, with Carl Foreman credited on the screenplay. I did not fetch a term record for the play or the translation.

editorial:
Cyrano de Bergerac (1950) was produced by Stanley Kramer Productions and released by United Artists. Michael Gordon directed, Carl Foreman wrote the screenplay from Brian Hooker's 1923 English translation of Rostand's play, and Dimitri Tiomkin wrote the score. José Ferrer won the Academy Award for Best Actor.

The rights trap is that the print's status is not proven here. For a work published in November 1950, the renewal window ran 1977 to 1978. A renewal filed in 1979 would have been a late filing, not part of the window. I found no 'Cyrano' entry in the part of the 1977 renewal catalog that my fetch returned, so that check is partial. I did not check the Jan-Jun 1978 or Jul-Dec 1978 catalogs, and I could not search the Copyright Office records. Claims that the film is in the public domain come from an uploader and from secondary reporting, and I did not verify them. Do the DIY search on all of these before you rely on the print. Tiomkin's score, the Hooker translation and the Rostand play each have their own copyright question, which this dossier did not resolve. Treat them as separate from the print.
faq: Was the 1950 Cyrano de Bergerac renewed?

Not confirmed. I found no entry in the part of the 1977 renewal catalog that I could read. I did not check the Jan-Jun 1978 or Jul-Dec 1978 catalogs, or the Copyright Office public records. Run those searches before relying on the print.
Does the score or the source play have its own rights?

Possibly. Dimitri Tiomkin's score and Brian Hooker's 1923 translation, which the screenplay uses, were not cleared in this research. A sound film's track normally shares the film's status, but check the music and translation separately.
